title: Metal Stud Wall STC Ratings: Complete 2026 Guide
description: Understand metal stud wall STC ratings: proven assemblies, resilient channel, mineral wool, decoupling, and airtight details. Built for Ontario & US jobs.
html:
Last updated: October 2026

Key takeaway:

Metal stud wall STC ratings belong to the complete wall assembly, not to the stud alone. Higher ratings usually come from combining more gypsum-board mass, cavity insulation, resilient channel or other decoupling, and airtight perimeter and penetration detailing; the selected tested assembly must also suit the adjoining floor, ceiling, and wall construction.

Sound Transmission Class (STC) helps designers and contractors compare how effectively a wall assembly reduces airborne sound such as speech, television, and office activity. For a metal stud wall, the result depends on the entire build-up: stud size and spacing, gypsum-board layers, cavity depth, insulation, resilient channel or clips, fasteners, junctions, and flanking paths.

What do metal stud wall STC ratings measure?

STC is a single-number laboratory rating for airborne sound transmission through a tested partition. A higher number generally means less speech and other mid-frequency sound passes through the wall, but it does not describe every acoustic problem. Low-frequency music, impact noise, doors, mechanical systems, and sound travelling around the wall require additional design attention.

The most important qualification is that STC is assigned to an assembly. A 3-5/8-inch steel stud does not have an STC rating by itself. The rating applies to the combination of studs, track, board, insulation, resilient components, fasteners, perimeter treatment, and associated construction tested together.

Laboratory results should therefore be used as a design reference rather than a guaranteed field score. Flanking through a ceiling plenum, floor, shaft, corridor bulkhead, electrical boxes, or an unsealed head-of-wall joint can reduce the performance of an otherwise well-selected assembly.

How should you read an STC rating?

Use an STC value to compare complete wall options against the privacy requirement for the space. It is not a promise that occupants will perceive every sound as equally quiet, and it is not a substitute for reviewing the tested construction details.

  • STC in the 30s: a basic light partition may reduce some speech but usually provides limited privacy.
  • STC in the 40s: a practical range for many offices, corridors, and interior separations when detailing is controlled.
  • STC 50 and above: a common design direction for stronger speech privacy and dwelling-unit separation, subject to the applicable code and tested assembly.
  • Higher than STC 55: typically requires greater separation between faces, more mass, resilient mounting, or a combination of these measures.

These ranges are planning guidance, not blanket compliance claims. For Canadian housing applications, the CCMC evaluation for a selected assembly states that the listed wall must be used with adjoining construction that meets the relevant prescriptive requirements. Review the CCMC wall-assembly evaluation and project-specific code requirements before issuing a submittal.

Which design choices improve a metal stud wall’s STC?

Reliable acoustic performance comes from several complementary controls. Increasing only one feature can help, but it may not address the dominant transmission path on a particular project.

1. Add mass with gypsum board

More gypsum-board layers increase surface mass and can improve transmission loss. Two layers on one or both sides may outperform a single layer, especially when joints are staggered and the board is fastened according to the tested design. Board type, thickness, screw pattern, and joint treatment all matter.

2. Absorb energy in the cavity

Mineral wool or another specified cavity insulation reduces sound energy inside the stud space. Install batts full height and without damaging, compressing, or leaving open gaps around services. Insulation is helpful, but it cannot compensate for a direct rigid connection or an open perimeter.

3. Decouple the wall faces

Resilient channel, isolation clips with hat channel, staggered studs, and independent double-stud walls interrupt vibration paths. The choice depends on available wall thickness, structural movement, installation tolerance, and the precise tested assembly.

Resilient channel only works as intended when the gypsum is attached to the channel rather than directly to the studs. An overlong screw, misplaced fastener, or service installation that bridges the channel can create a rigid short circuit.

4. Seal air paths and control flanking

Sound follows air leaks and alternate paths. Apply compatible acoustic sealant continuously at floor, head, and vertical edges, and seal around pipes, conduits, boxes, and other penetrations. Extend the separation to the deck where required, or detail the ceiling and bulkhead junction so sound cannot bypass the partition.

What are common metal stud wall STC assembly options?

The table below shows useful planning patterns. The figures are indicative ranges rather than certified ratings for every product combination. A project submittal should identify the exact tested assembly, component dimensions, board layers, insulation, fasteners, and installation requirements.

Assembly directionTypical componentsPlanning rangeBest fit
Basic single-stud wallSingle stud line with one gypsum layer on each sideMid-30sLow-privacy interior partitions
Insulated single-stud wallSingle stud line, cavity insulation, gypsum on both facesHigh-30s to low-40sGeneral offices and room divisions
Resilient-channel wallCavity insulation with resilient channel on one side and specified board layersMid-40s to around 50Speech privacy where wall thickness is limited
Higher-mass single-stud wallAdditional gypsum layers, insulation, and carefully sealed edgesAround 50 to mid-50sMore demanding office, clinic, or residential separations
Staggered-stud wallOffset studs on a wider track with a deeper insulated cavityAround 50 to mid-50sWhen separation is available without two independent tracks
Double-stud wallIndependent stud rows with an air gap, insulation, and multiple board layersMid-50s and higherHigh privacy and stronger decoupling requirements

As an evidence-based example, the USG UL U419 assembly listed in the supplied reference uses 5/8-inch Firecode X panels on both sides, 3-5/8-inch steel studs at 16 inches on centre, and fiberglass insulation, with a system STC of 45. That result belongs to the complete listed assembly and should not be generalized to every wall using similar studs.

Canadian guidance also identifies single steel-stud walls, resilient-channel configurations, and double-stud walls with a separation gap as relevant sound-control approaches. The federal guide on controlling sound transmission through gypsum-board walls describes increasing board layers, cavity depth, insulation, and separation as practical design measures.

How do you choose the right assembly?

Start with the acoustic goal and the constraints rather than selecting a product in isolation. A wall for an exam room may prioritize speech privacy, while a demising wall may also need fire, structural, moisture, and code performance.

  1. Define the occupied spaces. Identify whether the wall separates dwelling units, hotel rooms, offices, classrooms, clinics, corridors, or noisy service areas.
  2. Set the required performance. Confirm the project specification, applicable code, and whether the target is a laboratory STC, a field expectation, or both.
  3. Check available thickness. A double-stud or staggered-stud option may perform well acoustically but consume more floor area than a single-stud wall with resilient mounting.
  4. Review movement. Where structure can deflect, use an appropriate slotted deflection track and preserve the acoustic separation through the head-of-wall detail.
  5. Coordinate services. Offset electrical boxes, avoid back-to-back penetrations, and close shafts, bulkheads, and ceiling voids that could flank the wall.
  6. Specify the tested details. Do not substitute board, insulation, channel, screw length, or spacing without confirming that the change remains acceptable.

For component selection and framing terminology, the metal stud framing guide provides useful background. You can also review steel stud types and gauges before coordinating the acoustic assembly with structural and installation requirements.

What should installers verify in the field?

Many acoustic failures are workmanship failures rather than failures of the concept. A short pre-board inspection can catch issues while they are still accessible.

  • Confirm stud size, gauge, spacing, track type, and wall alignment against the approved drawing.
  • Install cavity insulation continuously and avoid voids, excessive compression, or service gaps.
  • Verify resilient channel orientation, spacing, and attachment. Keep gypsum fasteners short enough to avoid contacting the studs where the assembly requires isolation.
  • Apply a continuous seal at floor, head, and end conditions. Treat corners and changes in substrate as part of the same air barrier.
  • Offset boxes and protect them with the specified acoustic treatment. Seal pipes, conduits, and access points.
  • Inspect above ceilings, at shafts, around doors, and behind millwork for flanking paths.
  • Photograph concealed work and retain product data with the project closeout records.

Use the metal stud framing sizes guide when coordinating dimensions and spacing, and consult the drywall and metal studs guide for board-layer and joint-layout considerations. These resources support planning; the approved tested assembly remains the controlling reference.

Frequently Asked Questions

What STC should a metal stud demising wall achieve?

Many residential demising-wall designs use STC 50 as a laboratory target, with field performance affected by adjoining construction and flanking. The correct requirement depends on the applicable code, project specification, and selected tested assembly, so confirm the wall and its floor, ceiling, and junction details together.

Does resilient channel improve metal stud wall STC?

It can improve performance by separating the gypsum board from the stud line, but only when installed as part of a tested system. Direct fasteners, incorrect orientation, unsuitable spacing, or penetrations that bridge the channel can significantly reduce the benefit.

Is mineral wool enough to make a wall soundproof?

No. Mineral wool absorbs sound in the cavity, but it does not make a partition soundproof and cannot replace mass, decoupling, or airtight detailing. The wall should be designed as a complete assembly with its services and adjoining construction included.

Why can a wall with a good laboratory STC perform poorly on site?

Field performance can be reduced by flanking through ceilings, floors, shafts, doors, outlets, pipe penetrations, and unsealed perimeters. Installation substitutions and resilient-channel short circuits can also change the tested construction, so inspect concealed work and preserve the specified details.

Plan the complete assembly before framing

Metal stud wall STC ratings are most useful when treated as a complete-system decision. Compare the required privacy with wall thickness, movement, services, code requirements, and installation controls; then select a documented assembly and inspect the details that protect its performance.
